tests.title: Unit 7: Bank Reconciliation Statement – Practice Test 1

questions.question_text: A bank reconciliation statement (BRS) is:
options: A statement reconciling the cash book bank balance with the pass book balance
questions.explanation: It explains why the two balances differ.

questions.question_text: A BRS is prepared to:
options: Find the reasons for the difference between the cash book and pass book balances and detect errors

questions.question_text: The BRS is prepared by:
questions.explanation: The bank issues the pass book/statement.

questions.question_text: A BRS is:
questions.explanation: It is not a part of the double entry system.

questions.question_text: A pass book is:
options: A copy of the customer's account in the bank's books
questions.explanation: It is supplied by the bank.

questions.question_text: A bank statement is:
options: A periodic statement of the account issued by the bank
questions.explanation: It is the modern form of the pass book.

questions.question_text: The cash book differs from the pass book in that the cash book is:
options: Maintained by the business, the pass book by the bank
questions.explanation: They record the same transactions from different viewpoints.

questions.question_text: A debit balance in the cash book (bank column) shows:
A credit balance in the cash book (bank column) shows:
A debit balance in the pass book shows:
questions.explanation: The bank's record is the opposite of the firm's.

questions.question_text: A credit balance in the pass book shows:
options: Money available with the bank in favour of the customer

questions.question_text: The bank records deposits as _____ and withdrawals as _____ in its books for the customer's account:
questions.explanation: The bank is the debtor to the customer.

questions.question_text: Reasons for differences between the cash book and pass book include:
options: Timing differences, items not recorded by one party, and errors
questions.explanation: They can be cleared by a BRS.

questions.question_text: Outstanding (unpresented) cheques are:
options: Cheques issued by the firm but not yet presented to the bank for payment
questions.explanation: The bank has not yet debited them.

questions.question_text: Uncleared cheques are:
options: Cheques deposited by the firm but not yet credited by the bank
questions.explanation: The bank has not yet collected the proceeds.

questions.question_text: A post-dated cheque is:
options: A cheque dated in the future and not payable until that date, so not credited earlier
A cheque dated in the past
questions.explanation: It is not considered in the BRS until the date.

questions.question_text: Bank charges create a difference because:
options: The bank debits them to the account, and the firm records them later
questions.explanation: The cash book is adjusted afterwards.

questions.question_text: Bank interest creates a difference because:
options: The bank credits it to the account and the firm records it later
questions.explanation: The cash book is adjusted afterwards.

questions.question_text: A direct deposit by a customer creates a difference because:
options: The bank credits it but the firm learns about it later
questions.explanation: It appears in the pass book first.

questions.question_text: Standing instructions (e.g., insurance, loan EMI) paid by the bank:
options: Appear in the cash book first
Appear in the pass book but not yet in the cash book

questions.question_text: A dishonoured cheque creates a difference because:
options: The bank debits the customer, while the firm still shows the deposit in its cash book
questions.explanation: The firm learns of dishonour later.

questions.question_text: Timing differences are:
options: Differences caused by cheques recorded in one book earlier than in the other
questions.explanation: They reverse in the next period.

questions.question_text: Errors create a difference when:
options: Either the firm or the bank records a wrong amount

questions.question_text: When the starting balance is an overdraft, items that were added with a favourable balance are:
options: Deducted, and those deducted are added (signs are reversed)
questions.explanation: An overdraft is a negative balance.

questions.question_text: Starting with a favourable cash book balance, the items to add are:
options: Cheques issued not presented, interest and direct deposits credited by the bank
questions.explanation: These increase the pass book balance.

tests.title: Unit 7: Bank Reconciliation Statement – Practice Test 2

questions.question_text: Starting with a favourable cash book balance, the items to deduct are:
options: Cheques deposited not collected, bank charges and dishonoured cheques
questions.explanation: These reduce the pass book balance.

questions.question_text: Starting with a favourable pass book balance, the items to add are:
options: Cheques deposited but not yet collected
questions.explanation: These are already in the cash book.

questions.question_text: Starting with a favourable pass book balance, the items to deduct are:
options: Cheques issued but not yet presented
questions.explanation: These are already in the cash book.

questions.question_text: An adjusted cash book is:
options: A cash book updated for items found in the pass book before preparing the BRS

questions.question_text: The adjustment entry for bank charges Rs 200 is:
options: Bank Charges A/c Dr to Bank A/c

questions.question_text: The adjustment entry for interest credited by the bank Rs 500 is:
options: Bank A/c Dr to Interest Received A/c

questions.question_text: The adjustment entry for a direct deposit Rs 1,500 is:
options: Bank A/c Dr to Customer's A/c

questions.question_text: The adjustment entry for a dishonoured cheque Rs 2,000 is:
options: Customer's A/c Dr to Bank A/c

questions.question_text: The adjustment entry for insurance premium paid by the bank Rs 4,000 is:
options: Insurance A/c Dr to Bank A/c

questions.question_text: The first step in preparing a BRS is to:
options: Compare the cash book and pass book entries and note the differences

A cheque of Rs 5,000 was recorded as Rs 500 in the cash book (payment). The cash book balance is overstated by:
questions.explanation: Credit should have been 5,000 but was 500.

questions.question_text: PB balance Rs 70,000; wrong credit by the bank Rs 4,000; cheques deposited not credited Rs 6,000. The cash book balance is:
CB balance Rs 15,000; cheque issued to X Rs 2,000 not recorded in the cash book; bank interest Rs 300. The adjusted cash book balance is:

options: Not yet recorded and should be debited to Interest A/c and credited to Bank A/c

tests.title: Unit 7: Bank Reconciliation Statement – Practice Test 3

questions.question_text: CB balance Rs 9,000; cheques issued Rs 1,000 not presented. The pass book balance is:
PB balance Rs 14,000; cheque issued not presented Rs 3,000; cheque deposited not collected Rs 2,000. The cash book balance is:
PB Rs 50,000; CB Rs 46,000; the only difference is unpresented cheques, which total:
CB overdraft Rs 10,000 and unpresented cheques Rs 3,000. The pass book shows an overdraft of:
Outstanding cheques are added to the cash book balance to reach the pass book balance because:
options: The cash book has already deducted them but the bank has not yet
The bank has already deducted them
questions.explanation: The bank balance is still higher.

questions.question_text: Uncleared cheques are deducted from the cash book balance because:
options: The cash book has recorded the deposit but the bank has not yet credited it
questions.explanation: The bank balance is still lower.

questions.question_text: Bank charges are deducted from a favourable cash book balance because:
options: The bank has debited them but the cash book has not
The cash book has deducted them
questions.explanation: The pass book balance is lower.

questions.question_text: A dishonoured cheque does not appear in the cash book initially because:
options: The firm learns of dishonour only after the bank informs it
The bank does not record it
questions.explanation: The cash book still shows the deposit.

questions.question_text: A BRS and updating the cash book:
options: Serve different purposes: BRS explains differences, updating corrects the cash book

questions.question_text: The effect of a BRS on the balance sheet's bank balance is that it:
options: Confirms the correct (adjusted cash book) balance to be shown
questions.explanation: The balance sheet uses the adjusted cash book balance.

questions.question_text: The balance sheet shows the:
questions.explanation: It reflects the firm's own records.

questions.question_text: A BRS helps detect fraud because:
options: Unmatched items and unusual differences can be investigated

questions.question_text: A BRS should be prepared:
A limitation of a BRS is that it:
options: Does not prove all errors have been detected

questions.question_text: A bank error found in a BRS is:
options: Reported to the bank for correction, and shown as a reconciling item
questions.explanation: The cash book is not adjusted.

questions.question_text: A cheque dishonoured due to insufficient funds is treated by:
options: Debiting the customer's account and crediting bank in the cash book

questions.question_text: NEFT/RTGS receipts not recorded in the cash book cause:
options: A difference, as the bank has credited the amount and the cash book needs to record it

questions.question_text: An internal-control benefit of a BRS is that it:
options: Ensures bank records match the books and prevents misuse

questions.question_text: The BRS does not change the cash book balance unless:
options: Adjustments are made in the cash book

questions.question_text: The BRS does not change the pass book balance because:
A cheque of Rs 5,000 deposited on 30 March and credited by the bank on 2 April appears on 31 March:
options: In the cash book but not in the pass book (deducted from the CB balance in BRS)
In the pass book but not in the cash book

questions.question_text: A cheque issued on 28 March and presented on 3 April appears on 31 March:
options: In the cash book but not in the pass book (added to the CB balance in BRS)

questions.question_text: The date of presentation matters because:
options: The bank debits or credits the account only on that date

questions.question_text: A stale cheque is:
options: A cheque not presented within its validity of three months
questions.explanation: The bank will not honour it.

questions.question_text: An account-payee cheque differs from a bearer cheque in that it:
options: Can only be credited to the payee's account, while a bearer cheque is payable to the holder

tests.title: Unit 7: Bank Reconciliation Statement – Practice Test 4

questions.question_text: A stop-payment instruction to the bank:
options: Prevents payment of a cheque issued, which is added back in the cash book

questions.question_text: Documents needed to prepare a BRS include:
options: Cash book (bank column) and the pass book/bank statement

questions.question_text: A BRS is prepared for:
options: Any bank account (current, savings, overdraft, etc.)
questions.explanation: Wherever the cash book and bank records exist.

questions.question_text: A standing instruction for loan EMI is:
options: Recorded in the cash book first
Recorded by the bank first and later recorded in the cash book

questions.question_text: Interest on fixed deposit credited by the bank is:
options: Income, recorded in the cash book after being seen in the pass book

questions.question_text: A mandate is:
options: An instruction by the customer to the bank to pay amounts, which appears in the pass book

questions.question_text: At year end, an uncleared cheque is:
options: Shown in the cash book as a deposit and appears in the BRS as a reconciling item
questions.explanation: The balance sheet shows the cash book balance.

questions.question_text: In a BRS for an account with an overdraft limit, the overdraft is treated:
options: As a negative balance with signs reversed

questions.question_text: Window dressing with cheques means:
options: Showing higher bank balances by recording cheques as received/not issued at year-end; the BRS detects it by comparing with the bank statement

questions.question_text: A practical BRS case: a firm's cash book shows Rs 50,000 but the bank statement shows Rs 55,000. The difference may be due to:
options: Cheques issued not yet presented, etc.

questions.question_text: A cheque issued on 31 March and presented on 5 April means the bank statement balance on 31 March is:
options: Lower than the cash book balance
Higher than the cash book balance
questions.explanation: The bank has not yet debited it.

questions.question_text: A BRS is needed even when both the cash book and pass book are correct because:
If there are uncleared cheques, the bank balance shown in the balance sheet is:

PB balance Rs 36,500; cheques issued not presented 8,000; dishonoured cheque 1,000 not in the cash book. The cash book balance is:
CB balance Rs 5,000; cheques deposited not credited 2,000; insurance paid by the bank 600; interest 150. The pass book balance is:
CB overdraft Rs 12,000; cheques issued not presented 4,000; interest on overdraft 300 not recorded. The pass book overdraft is:

A post-dated cheque received but not yet deposited is:
options: Not considered in the BRS until its date arrives
questions.explanation: It has no effect on the bank balance until presented.

questions.question_text: The bank statement should be matched regularly with the cash book to:
options: Detect errors and fraud early and keep records accurate

questions.question_text: A bank reconciliation differs from a bank statement in that the bank statement is:
options: Issued by the bank, while the reconciliation is prepared by the firm to explain differences

questions.question_text: NEFT/UPI credits in reconciliation are:
options: Matched with the cash book; those not recorded in the cash book are adjusted
questions.explanation: Check each credit against sales or receipts.
